blocks.en: Genesis Intensive — Unit 5: Walking With God and the Nations — Enoch, Noah and Babel
blocks.es_reference: Intensivo de Génesis — Unidad 5: Caminando con Dios y las Naciones — Enoc, Noé y Babel

blocks.en: “And Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him.” — Genesis 5:24 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: “Caminó, pues, Enoc con Dios, y desapareció, porque le llevó Dios.” — Génesis 5:24 (RVG)

blocks.en: The Refrain of Death and the Exception of Enoch
blocks.es_reference: El Estribillo de la Muerte y la Excepción de Enoc

blocks.en: Genesis 5 is deliberately repetitive. Generation follows generation, years accumulate, children are born, and then the same conclusion returns: “and he died.” The repetition forces the reader to feel the consequence of the Fall across time. Against that dark refrain stands Enoch. His life is described with unusual simplicity: “Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him.” The center of his story is not longevity, achievement, or public prominence but fellowship with God.
blocks.es_reference: Génesis 5 es repetitivo a propósito. Una generación sigue a otra, se acumulan los años, nacen hijos y vuelve la misma conclusión: «y murió». La repetición obliga al lector a sentir el peso de la Caída a lo largo del tiempo. Frente a ese oscuro estribillo aparece Enoc. Su vida se describe con una sencillez poco común: «Caminó, pues, Enoc con Dios, y desapareció, porque le llevó Dios». El centro de su historia no es la longevidad, los logros ni la notoriedad pública, sino la comunión con Dios.

blocks.en: Walking as a Direction of Life
blocks.es_reference: Caminar como Dirección de Vida

blocks.en: In Scripture, walking commonly describes a settled direction or manner of life. To walk with God is therefore more than enjoying occasional religious experiences. It means living consciously before Him in faith, obedience, fellowship, and continuing dependence. Hebrews 11 connects Enoch with faith and with pleasing God. The emphasis should not be turned into a claim of sinless perfection; the biblical picture is a life oriented toward God rather than a life that merely visits Him in moments of crisis.
blocks.es_reference: En la Escritura, caminar suele describir una dirección o una manera de vivir ya establecida. Por tanto, caminar con Dios es más que disfrutar de experiencias religiosas ocasionales. Significa vivir conscientemente delante de Él en fe, obediencia, comunión y dependencia continua. Hebreos 11 relaciona a Enoc con la fe y con agradar a Dios. Este énfasis no debe convertirse en una afirmación de perfección sin pecado; el cuadro bíblico es el de una vida orientada hacia Dios, y no el de una vida que solo lo visita en momentos de crisis.

blocks.en: Faith in a Dark World
blocks.es_reference: Fe en un Mundo Oscuro

blocks.en: Enoch’s faithfulness is striking because Genesis does not place him in an ideal environment. The chapters surrounding his genealogy move toward increasing violence and corruption. Faithfulness is therefore not dependent upon living in a society that supports it. Believers may have to walk with God when the surrounding culture moves in another direction. The answer is neither withdrawal into contempt for the world nor surrender to it, but a life whose deepest loyalty belongs to God.
blocks.es_reference: La fidelidad de Enoc llama la atención porque Génesis no lo sitúa en un ambiente ideal. Los capítulos que rodean su genealogía avanzan hacia una violencia y una corrupción cada vez mayores. Por tanto, la fidelidad no depende de vivir en una sociedad que la favorezca. Puede que los creyentes tengan que caminar con Dios mientras la cultura que los rodea va en otra dirección. La respuesta no es retirarse con desprecio del mundo ni rendirse a él, sino llevar una vida cuya lealtad más profunda pertenezca a Dios.

blocks.en: The Hope in “God Took Him”
blocks.es_reference: La Esperanza en «Dios le Llevó»

blocks.en: Enoch’s departure interrupts the ordinary formula of Genesis 5. The text does not describe the mechanics in detail, and speculation should not replace what is actually said. Hebrews 11:5 interprets Enoch as translated so that he did not see death. His story therefore gives a brief but powerful witness that death does not possess the final word over those who belong to God. Later revelation will develop resurrection and eternal life far more fully, but even here the rhythm of death is interrupted by divine action.
blocks.es_reference: La partida de Enoc interrumpe la fórmula habitual de Génesis 5. El texto no describe en detalle cómo ocurrió, y la especulación no debe reemplazar lo que realmente dice. Hebreos 11:5 interpreta que Enoc fue trasladado para no ver muerte. Así, su historia ofrece un testimonio breve pero poderoso de que la muerte no tiene la última palabra sobre quienes pertenecen a Dios. La revelación posterior desarrollará mucho más plenamente la resurrección y la vida eterna, pero ya aquí una acción divina interrumpe el ritmo de la muerte.

blocks.en: Noah Also Walked With God
blocks.es_reference: Noé También Caminó con Dios

blocks.en: The same expression appears again when Genesis introduces Noah as a righteous man who “walked with God.” Unit 4 emphasized that Noah first “found grace in the eyes of the LORD,” so his walk should not be treated as self-produced merit that forced God to save him. Grace and responsive faithfulness belong together. Noah’s obedience in building the ark becomes visible evidence of a life that takes God’s word seriously even when obedience is costly and the surrounding world is corrupt.
blocks.es_reference: La misma expresión vuelve a aparecer cuando Génesis presenta a Noé como un hombre justo que «con Dios caminó». La Unidad 4 destacó que primero Noé «halló gracia en los ojos de Jehová», de modo que su caminar no debe tratarse como un mérito propio que obligó a Dios a salvarlo. La gracia y la fidelidad que responde a ella van juntas. La obediencia de Noé al construir el arca se convierte en una prueba visible de una vida que toma en serio la palabra de Dios, aun cuando obedecer cuesta y el mundo que lo rodea está corrompido.

blocks.en: Grace Does Not End the Need to Walk
blocks.es_reference: La Gracia no Elimina la Necesidad de Caminar

blocks.en: The Flood does not produce a morally perfect human race. Noah himself later fails, and Genesis says that the inclination of the human heart remains evil. The answer to the human problem cannot therefore be merely a new environment. Walking with God remains necessary after judgment just as before it. External reform, social organization, and technological progress may accomplish real good, but none can substitute for the transformation and fellowship with God that the biblical story increasingly shows humanity needs.
blocks.es_reference: El Diluvio no produce una raza humana moralmente perfecta. Noé mismo falla después, y Génesis dice que la inclinación del corazón humano sigue siendo mala. Por tanto, la respuesta al problema humano no puede ser simplemente un entorno nuevo. Caminar con Dios sigue siendo tan necesario después del juicio como antes. La reforma externa, la organización social y el progreso tecnológico pueden lograr bienes reales, pero ninguno de ellos puede sustituir la transformación y la comunión con Dios que, como la historia bíblica muestra cada vez más, la humanidad necesita.

blocks.en: From One Family to Many Nations
blocks.es_reference: De Una Familia a Muchas Naciones

blocks.en: Genesis 10 widens the camera from Noah’s family to the peoples and nations. The table of nations is theological geography rather than a modern ethnic census. It reminds the reader that humanity remains one family while spreading into distinct peoples, lands, and languages. The nations are not incidental to God’s purpose. Genesis is preparing for a redemptive promise that will deliberately include “all the families of the earth.”
blocks.es_reference: Génesis 10 amplía el enfoque desde la familia de Noé hacia los pueblos y las naciones. La tabla de las naciones es geografía teológica y no un censo étnico moderno. Recuerda al lector que la humanidad sigue siendo una sola familia mientras se extiende en distintos pueblos, tierras e idiomas. Las naciones no son algo secundario en el propósito de Dios. Génesis está preparando una promesa redentora que incluirá deliberadamente a «todas las familias de la tierra».

blocks.en: Babel — Unity Without Submission
blocks.es_reference: Babel — Unidad sin Sumisión

blocks.en: Genesis 11 begins with human unity, but unity itself is not automatically righteous. The people settle together, build a city and tower, and declare, “let us make a name for ourselves.” Their project expresses collective self-exaltation and resistance to the divine purpose that humanity fill the earth. Babel therefore warns that human cooperation can become organized rebellion when common purpose is detached from submission to God. The problem is not architecture, urban life, or technology; it is proud autonomy.
blocks.es_reference: Génesis 11 comienza con la unidad humana, pero la unidad en sí misma no es automáticamente justa. La gente se establece en un mismo lugar, edifica una ciudad y una torre, y declara: «hagámonos un nombre». Su proyecto expresa una autoexaltación colectiva y una resistencia al propósito divino de que la humanidad llene la tierra. Así, Babel advierte que la cooperación humana puede convertirse en rebelión organizada cuando el propósito común se desliga de la sumisión a Dios. El problema no es la arquitectura, la vida urbana ni la tecnología; es la autonomía orgullosa.

blocks.en: “Let Us Make a Name”
blocks.es_reference: «Hagámonos un Nombre»

blocks.en: The desire to make a name provides an important bridge to Abraham. Babel seeks security and significance through human concentration and self-made greatness. In Genesis 12, by contrast, God tells Abraham, “I will bless you and make your name great.” The contrast is not that having a recognized name is inherently sinful. The issue is whether significance is seized in proud independence or received as part of God’s gracious calling and mission.
blocks.es_reference: El deseo de hacerse un nombre tiende un puente importante hacia Abraham. Babel busca seguridad e importancia mediante la concentración humana y una grandeza fabricada por sí misma. En cambio, en Génesis 12 Dios dice a Abraham: «te bendeciré, y engrandeceré tu nombre». El contraste no consiste en que tener un nombre reconocido sea pecaminoso en sí mismo. La cuestión es si la importancia se arrebata con orgullosa independencia o se recibe como parte del llamamiento y la misión que Dios da por gracia.

blocks.en: God Comes Down
blocks.es_reference: Dios Desciende

blocks.en: The builders intend a tower whose top reaches toward heaven, yet Genesis says that the LORD “came down” to see the city and tower. The irony is deliberate. What appears enormous from the human perspective is not a threat to divine sovereignty. Human pride regularly exaggerates its own scale. Babel is not a contest between nearly equal powers; it is a story in which the Creator effortlessly exposes the limits of collective human self-exaltation.
blocks.es_reference: Los constructores se proponen levantar una torre cuya cúspide llegue al cielo, pero Génesis dice que Jehová «descendió» para ver la ciudad y la torre. La ironía es deliberada. Lo que parece enorme desde la perspectiva humana no amenaza la soberanía divina. El orgullo humano suele exagerar su propia magnitud. Babel no es una contienda entre poderes casi iguales; es una historia en la que el Creador deja al descubierto, sin esfuerzo alguno, los límites de la autoexaltación humana colectiva.

blocks.en: Confusion and Scattering
blocks.es_reference: Confusión y Dispersión

blocks.en: God confuses their language and scatters them. Genesis presents this as judgment upon the rebellious project, but the scattering also accomplishes what the builders resisted: humanity spreads over the earth. The passage should not be made to carry claims it does not need to carry about the detailed scientific origin of every language family. Its theological message is clear without such overstatement: proud humanity seeks centralized self-glory, and God frustrates the rebellion while continuing His purpose for the nations.
blocks.es_reference: Dios confunde su lengua y los dispersa. Génesis presenta esto como un juicio sobre el proyecto rebelde, pero la dispersión también logra aquello a lo que los constructores se resistían: que la humanidad se extienda por la tierra. No hay que cargar al pasaje con afirmaciones que no necesita sobre el origen científico detallado de cada familia de lenguas. Su mensaje teológico es claro sin tales exageraciones: la humanidad orgullosa busca una gloria propia centralizada, y Dios frustra la rebelión mientras sigue adelante con su propósito para las naciones.

blocks.en: Babel Leads to Abraham
blocks.es_reference: Babel Conduce a Abraham

blocks.en: Genesis does not leave the reader among scattered nations without hope. The genealogy after Babel narrows toward Abram, and Genesis 12 immediately announces a promise whose horizon is worldwide: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” God answers the problem of the nations not by abandoning them but by calling one man and family through whom blessing will move outward. Election in Genesis is therefore connected with mission. Abraham is chosen by grace to become a channel of blessing rather than a private owner of divine favor.
blocks.es_reference: Génesis no deja al lector sin esperanza entre naciones dispersas. La genealogía posterior a Babel se va estrechando hacia Abram, y Génesis 12 anuncia de inmediato una promesa de horizonte mundial: «serán benditas en ti todas las familias de la tierra». Dios responde al problema de las naciones no abandonándolas, sino llamando a un hombre y a una familia por medio de quienes la bendición se extenderá hacia afuera. Por tanto, en Génesis la elección está unida a la misión. Abraham es escogido por gracia para ser un canal de bendición, y no el dueño exclusivo del favor divino.

blocks.en: Pentecost and the Barrier of Babel
blocks.es_reference: Pentecostés y la Barrera de Babel

blocks.en: Pentecost can appropriately be described as a redemptive reversal of Babel, provided the comparison is stated carefully. At Babel, language becomes a barrier associated with scattering and rebellious human self-exaltation. At Pentecost, the Spirit enables people from many nations to hear the mighty works of God in their own languages. Pentecost does not erase languages, nations, or cultural distinctions. Instead, God overcomes the linguistic barrier for gospel proclamation and gathers a people around Christ without requiring humanity to become culturally uniform.
blocks.es_reference: Es apropiado describir Pentecostés como una reversión redentora de Babel, siempre que la comparación se exprese con cuidado. En Babel, el idioma se convierte en una barrera ligada a la dispersión y a la autoexaltación humana rebelde. En Pentecostés, el Espíritu permite que personas de muchas naciones oigan las maravillas de Dios en sus propios idiomas. Pentecostés no borra los idiomas, las naciones ni las diferencias culturales. Más bien, Dios vence la barrera lingüística para la proclamación del evangelio y reúne a un pueblo en torno a Cristo sin exigir que la humanidad se vuelva culturalmente uniforme.

blocks.en: From Pentecost to the Great Commission
blocks.es_reference: De Pentecostés a la Gran Comisión

blocks.en: The line from Babel through Abraham reaches beyond Acts 2. The risen Christ commands His disciples to make disciples of all nations. What was promised to Abraham moves outward through Christ and the gospel to the peoples of the world. The church therefore cannot treat missions as an optional department for unusually adventurous Christians. The multinational purpose of God is woven into the biblical story from Genesis onward.
blocks.es_reference: La línea que va de Babel a Abraham llega más allá de Hechos 2. Cristo resucitado manda a sus discípulos hacer discípulos a todas las naciones. Lo prometido a Abraham avanza por medio de Cristo y del evangelio hacia los pueblos del mundo. Por tanto, la iglesia no puede tratar las misiones como un departamento opcional para cristianos excepcionalmente aventureros. El propósito de Dios para todas las naciones está entretejido en la historia bíblica desde Génesis en adelante.

blocks.en: Walking With God in a World of Self-Made Names
blocks.es_reference: Caminando con Dios en un Mundo de Nombres Fabricados

blocks.en: Enoch and Babel form a useful spiritual contrast. Enoch’s significance is summarized by his walk with God; Babel’s builders seek to manufacture significance by making a name for themselves. One life is oriented toward fellowship with God, while the other project is organized around collective self-exaltation. Ministry constantly faces the same choice. Churches and leaders can seek faithfulness before God or become preoccupied with visibility, reputation, numbers, platforms, and institutional names.
blocks.es_reference: Enoc y Babel forman un contraste espiritual útil. La importancia de Enoc se resume en su caminar con Dios; los constructores de Babel buscan fabricarse importancia haciéndose un nombre. Una vida está orientada hacia la comunión con Dios, mientras que el otro proyecto se organiza en torno a la autoexaltación colectiva. El ministerio se enfrenta constantemente a la misma elección. Las iglesias y los líderes pueden buscar la fidelidad delante de Dios o dejarse absorber por la visibilidad, la reputación, las cifras, las plataformas y los nombres institucionales.

blocks.en: The God of the Nations
blocks.es_reference: El Dios de las Naciones

blocks.en: Genesis 5–11 never allows the human actors to become ultimate. God takes Enoch, gives Noah grace, judges violence, preserves life, covenants with creation, scatters Babel, and directs the story toward Abraham. He is not a tribal deity whose concern begins only when Israel appears. He is Creator and Judge of all humanity and the God whose redemptive purpose embraces the nations. This is why the transition to Abraham is not a narrowing of divine concern but the beginning of a particular means for worldwide blessing.
blocks.es_reference: Génesis 5–11 nunca permite que los actores humanos ocupen el lugar supremo. Dios lleva a Enoc, da gracia a Noé, juzga la violencia, preserva la vida, hace pacto con la creación, dispersa a los de Babel y dirige la historia hacia Abraham. No es una deidad tribal cuyo interés comienza solo cuando aparece Israel. Es el Creador y Juez de toda la humanidad, y el Dios cuyo propósito redentor abarca a las naciones. Por eso el paso a Abraham no reduce el interés divino, sino que da comienzo a un medio particular para bendecir al mundo entero.

blocks.en: Ministry Application
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación Ministerial

blocks.en: Walking with God is not escape from a dark world but faithful life within it. Enoch walks while death surrounds his generation; Noah obeys amid corruption; the nations multiply; Babel organizes pride; and God continues His purpose. Christian ministry should form people whose identity rests in fellowship with God rather than in making a name, and churches whose vision reaches beyond their own language, nation, and culture. The gospel does not erase human diversity; it carries the blessing of Christ across those boundaries.
blocks.es_reference: Caminar con Dios no es escapar de un mundo oscuro, sino vivir fielmente dentro de él. Enoc camina mientras la muerte rodea a su generación; Noé obedece en medio de la corrupción; las naciones se multiplican; Babel organiza su orgullo; y Dios continúa su propósito. El ministerio cristiano debe formar personas cuya identidad descanse en la comunión con Dios y no en hacerse un nombre, e iglesias cuya visión llegue más allá de su propio idioma, nación y cultura. El evangelio no borra la diversidad humana; lleva la bendición de Cristo a través de esas fronteras.

blocks.en: Summary
blocks.es_reference: Resumen

blocks.en: Genesis moves from Enoch’s personal walk with God to Noah’s faithful obedience, from Noah’s family to the nations, and from the nations to Babel’s proud attempt at self-made unity. God judges and scatters, yet He does not abandon the nations. The story moves directly toward Abraham and the promise of blessing for all families of the earth, a trajectory Christians see reaching Christ, Pentecost, and the Great Commission. The choice between walking with God and making a name for ourselves remains spiritually searching, while behind the entire movement stands the almighty and holy God whose purpose reaches every nation.
blocks.es_reference: Génesis avanza del caminar personal de Enoc con Dios a la obediencia fiel de Noé, de la familia de Noé a las naciones, y de las naciones al orgulloso intento de Babel de fabricar su propia unidad. Dios juzga y dispersa, pero no abandona a las naciones. La historia avanza directamente hacia Abraham y la promesa de bendición para todas las familias de la tierra, una trayectoria que, según ven los cristianos, llega hasta Cristo, Pentecostés y la Gran Comisión. La elección entre caminar con Dios y hacernos un nombre sigue escudriñando el corazón, mientras detrás de todo este movimiento está el Dios todopoderoso y santo cuyo propósito alcanza a toda nación.

mc.stem: What distinguishes Enoch in Genesis 5?
options: He walked with God and God took him
He lived longer than anyone else in the line
He built a city named after his son
He was the father of Noah
mc.why: He walked with God and God took him.

mc.stem: What does “walking with God” primarily describe?
options: A state of sinless moral perfection
A physical journey to a sacred place
Occasional religious experiences in times of crisis
A continuing direction of life in faith and fellowship
mc.why: A continuing direction of life in faith and fellowship.

mc.stem: How does Hebrews 11 interpret Enoch?
options: As a man of faith who pleased God
As a sinless man who never needed grace
As a worshiper who offered a better sacrifice
As a builder who prepared an ark
mc.why: As a man of faith who pleased God.

mc.stem: What does Enoch’s departure interrupt?
options: The rising floodwaters of Genesis 7
The building of the tower in Genesis 11
The repeated Genesis 5 refrain of death
The listing of Cain's descendants in Genesis 4
mc.why: The repeated Genesis 5 refrain of death.

mc.stem: What does Noah share with Enoch?
options: He also was taken without dying
He also walked with God
He also was the seventh from Adam
He also built a city
mc.why: He also walked with God.

mc.stem: What precedes Noah’s obedience in Genesis 6?
options: Noah's own merit
The people's repentance
The rainbow sign
God’s grace
mc.why: God’s grace.

mc.stem: What is the broad function of Genesis 10?
options: To list the long-lived patriarchs before the Flood
To trace Cain's line down to Lamech
To show humanity spreading into peoples and nations
To give a modern ethnic census of every people
mc.why: To show humanity spreading into peoples and nations.

mc.stem: What is wrong at Babel?
options: Having too many different languages
Proud collective autonomy and self-exaltation
Architecture and the use of new technology
Neglecting to offer animal sacrifices
mc.why: Proud collective autonomy and self-exaltation.

mc.stem: What do Babel’s builders say they want to make?
options: A covenant with God
An altar to the LORD
A name for themselves
An ark for their families
mc.why: A name for themselves.

mc.stem: What ironic action does God take in Genesis 11?
options: He sends a flood to destroy the tower
He comes down to see the city and tower
He strikes the tower with fire from heaven
He sends an angel to warn the builders
mc.why: He comes down to see the city and tower.

mc.stem: What results from Babel?
options: Language confusion and scattering
Fire and brimstone on the city
The successful completion of the tower
A worldwide flood and a new covenant
mc.why: Language confusion and scattering.

mc.stem: What should not be forced from Babel?
options: A warning against collective pride and self-glory
The truth that God frustrates proud human rebellion
God's continuing purpose for the scattered nations
A detailed scientific account of every language family
mc.why: A detailed scientific account of every language family.

mc.stem: How does Abraham contrast with Babel?
options: God promises to make Abraham’s name great rather than Abraham manufacturing his own greatness
Abraham earns a great name through obedience rather than receiving it as a promise from God
Abraham refuses to have any name at all because being known is inherently sinful
Abraham gathers the scattered nations into one city rather than letting them spread out
mc.why: God promises to make Abraham’s name great rather than Abraham manufacturing his own greatness.

mc.stem: What worldwide promise follows Babel?
options: Only Abraham's household will be blessed by God
All nations will again speak one language
All families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham
The earth will not again be destroyed by a flood
mc.why: All families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham.

mc.stem: In what qualified sense does Pentecost reverse Babel?
options: The Spirit overcomes the language barrier for gospel proclamation
The apostles master every language through careful study
The Spirit merges every nation into one uniform culture
The Spirit restores one single language for all humanity
mc.why: The Spirit overcomes the language barrier for gospel proclamation.

mc.stem: What does Pentecost not do?
options: Let people hear God's works in their own languages
Overcome the language barrier for the gospel
Gather people from many nations around Christ
Erase languages, nations, or cultural distinctions
mc.why: Erase languages, nations, or cultural distinctions.

mc.stem: Where does the Babel-Abraham trajectory ultimately move in Christian reading?
options: Toward the Flood, the ark, and the rainbow
Toward a rebuilt tower and a single world city
Toward Israel alone and away from the nations
Toward Christ, Pentecost, and the Great Commission
mc.why: Toward Christ, Pentecost, and the Great Commission.

mc.stem: What spiritual contrast can be drawn between Enoch and Babel?
options: Quiet solitude versus busy city life
Walking with God versus making a name for ourselves
Building an ark versus building a tower
Long life versus early death
mc.why: Walking with God versus making a name for ourselves.

mc.stem: What does Genesis reveal about God’s concern for the nations?
options: He is a tribal deity concerned only with Israel
He takes interest in the nations only once the church appears
He is Creator, Judge, and the source of worldwide redemptive blessing
He abandons the nations after scattering them at Babel
mc.why: He is Creator, Judge, and the source of worldwide redemptive blessing.

mc.stem: What is the central movement of Unit 5?
options: Human cooperation achieves a unity that God finally approves at Babel
Walking with God leads into God’s purpose for the nations despite human pride
Enoch's example shows that faithfulness requires withdrawing from the world
The Flood removes human pride so the nations can flourish on their own
mc.why: Walking with God leads into God’s purpose for the nations despite human pride.

fill.prompt: Genesis 5 is deliberately repetitive: generation after generation ends with the same refrain, "and he ____."
"Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God ____ him."

Hebrews 11:5 interprets Enoch as ____ so that he did not see death.
Noah's walk was not self-produced merit, for he first "found ____ in the eyes of the LORD."
The table of nations in Genesis 10 is ____ rather than a modern ethnic census.
The builders of Babel declare, "let us make a ____ for ourselves."
The problem at Babel is not architecture, urban life, or technology; it is proud ____, people ruling themselves with no submission to God.
The builders intend a tower reaching toward heaven, yet Genesis says that the LORD "____" to see the city and tower.
Pentecost can appropriately be described as a redemptive ____ of Babel.

sa.prompt: Relate Noah’s grace and obedience to the idea of walking with God.
sa.model: A strong answer should integrate Noah, grace, obedience, walk, faith while keeping God’s grace, human responsibility, and the passage’s redemptive movement in view.

sa.prompt: Explain the sin of Babel without condemning technology, cities, or human cooperation themselves.
sa.model: A strong answer should integrate Babel, pride, autonomy, name, technology while keeping God’s grace, human responsibility, and the passage’s redemptive movement in view.

sa.prompt: Explain the theological meaning of God confusing language and scattering Babel.
